About panel judges A and B (both pass): they are right that ports are dynamic. They are also right that the entrance-motion e2e test spawns vite.js directly and kills it in afterAll. Their pass rests on `expectPortClosed`/`expectNoPreviewProcess`, but those checks run only after `run()` resolves (lines 62-67). On the timeout branch the promise rejects first, so the checks never execute. They therefore prove nothing about that exit path, and on it the test kills only the npm wrapper. Human review
#QuestionRatingRationale
1Across the full presentation, how good do the titles, captions, labels, and other content text look and read? Judge whether important content text is visibly present, typography, sizing, weight, spacing, line breaks, contrast, legibility, visual hierarchy, and whether the wording is clear, intentional, and audience-ready rather than sounding like an internal annotation. Do not judge navigation controls or presentation chrome here, and do not judge the placement or styling of non-text elements.4 / 5—
2How well designed are the individual scene elements, such as boxes, arrows, icons, illustrations, and diagram nodes? Judge their shapes, proportions, fills, borders, detail, consistency, and overall craft. Do not judge their text, placement, movement, or navigation chrome here.3 / 5poorly aligned arrows
3At a normal wide viewport, how well are the text and visual elements arranged relative to one another? Judge alignment, spacing, grouping, balance, focal points, use of space, and whether anything feels crowded, disconnected, clipped, or unintentionally overlapping. Judge viewport adaptation separately under responsive visual quality.4 / 5—
4As you advance through the presentation, how well do the animations and scene changes work? Judge smoothness, pacing, meaningful entrances and exits, continuity of persistent elements, and whether each step visibly evolves the existing scene instead of feeling like an unrelated replacement.4 / 5—
5Taken as a whole, how strong is the presentation’s visual identity? Judge its color palette, background treatment, stylistic consistency, brand character, polish, memorability, and whether it feels intentionally designed and finished. Judge the craft of individual scene elements separately.4 / 5—
6How clear, discoverable, and visually integrated are the presentation controls and chrome? Judge progress indicators, previous/next controls, table of contents, mode switching, and attribution. Focus on their appearance and ease of understanding, not whether every input method technically works or how content captions are styled.2 / 5placement is awful
7Compare the presentation at wide and narrow viewport sizes. How well does its hierarchy and composition adapt? Judge scaling, density, readability, control accessibility, clipping, overlap, and whether the narrow version still feels intentionally composed. Judge baseline wide-screen composition separately.4 / 5—

Stage computes key = step.groupKey ?? step.id. It renders a single motion.div keyed by that key and puts SceneComponent inside it, so moving between steps updates the same mounted scene instead of remounting. Identity: Scene.tsx gives each entity layoutId={entity(name)}, using the presentation-owned entity() helper from entities.ts. Stable names include you, prompt, skill, conversation, question, card-i, link-i, ghost, depth, kit, kit-plug, verify, verify-link, modify, flag and reveal. tiebreaks{"demo-integration":{"ok":true,"criteria":["demo-clear-code-boundaries"],"inventory_kind":"neutral source","attempts":[{"stage":"tiebreak","attempt":1,"ok":true,"error":null},{"stage":"tiebreak-recite","attempt":1,"ok":true,"error":null}],"first_results":[{"id":"demo-clear-code-boundaries","verdict":"fail","rationale":"The criterion requires that the public inputs and shared constants the demo relies on have real consumers. Any dead or misleading contract is scored here, even when it is declared in shared scene-kit source. The title contract is fine. Talk passes title to Presentation, and Presentation and Header render it in an h1, so the title is not the problem. The shared kit constants module exports EASE = [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1] and LAYOUT_T = 0.55 (src/presentation-kit/constants.ts:1-2). These read as the kit&#39;s layout-transition easing and duration contract, but nothing consumes either one. I searched the whole source for each name as a whole word, excluding lockfiles. The only matches are the declarations in src/presentation-kit/constants.ts and the bootstrap template copy. No file imports them, reads them as a member, or forwards them as a prop. The only files that import from constants are Stage.tsx (DESIGN_W, DESIGN_H, STAGE_LAYOUT), useFitScale.ts (DESIGN_W, DESIGN_H, MIN_SCALE) and Appear.tsx (ENTER_T, ENTER_DELAY). The layout nodes set only layout and layoutId, with no transition built from these constants (for example Box.tsx:3). Stage.tsx:29 hard-codes its own transition duration of 0.25. Its timeout handler (line 28) calls only `child.kill(&#39;SIGKILL&#39;)` on that npm wrapper and then rejects. SIGKILL on npm does not reach the verify or inspect script npm launched. Those scripts spawn their own Vite preview and Chromium (scripts/verify.mjs line 34), and their cleanup runs in a `finally` that is never reached when the wrapper is SIGKILLed. On that path the preview keeps running. The checks at lines 66-67 and 173 (expectPortClosed and expectNoPreviewProcess) run only after run() resolves, so they never cover the timeout path. afterAll (line 105) only removes temporary directories. Judge C&#39;s reason is borne out, so I rule C&#39;s fail. Judges A and B are correct that ports come from freePort() (e2e line 12; acceptance line 61; verify defaults to freePort at line 33) and that the e2e test spawns vite.js directly and SIGTERMs it. Line 45 then asserts the transition&#39;s settled end state, `samples.at(-1).opacity` toBe(1). The settled state is never waited for: the test waits a fixed time for the transition and then asserts the result. That is the fixed wait before asserting that the guidance names. The acceptance test does the same through the tool it drives. At lines 147-164 of scripts/integration-acceptance.test.ts it passes `--settle 650` and asserts `activeAnimations=0` on each capture. The inspect helper (scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs lines 58-63) reaches that state only through `page.waitForTimeout(settle)`, with no wait on a settled signal. Judge C&#39;s reason is borne out, so I rule C&#39;s fail. Judge A treats the 1400 ms loop as the measurement rather than a sleep before an assertion, but line 45 asserts the final settled opacity at the end of that fixed window, so the assertion still depends on elapsed time. Judge B says no fixed delay precedes the assertions, which the 1400 ms window and the `--settle 650` fixed wait contradict. No test code reaps the grandchild preview or browser. - The cited lines are the whole timeout branch: it kills only the npm wrapper and has no other termination. About panel judges A and B (both pass): they are right that ports are dynamic. They are also right that the entrance-motion e2e test spawns vite.js directly and kills it in afterAll. Their pass rests on `expectPortClosed`/`expectNoPreviewProcess`, but those checks run only after `run()` resolves (lines 62-67). On the timeout branch the promise rejects first, so the checks never execute. They therefore prove nothing about that exit path, and on it the test kills only the npm wrapper.
